📰 The Virtual Deal: Cash, Ceasefires, and 60 Days of Fog

A memorandum that may or may not be signed, on a date that may or may not matter, between parties that may or may not agree on what it says.

According to the Iranian version, the framework is straightforward: Tehran reopens the Strait of Hormuz; Washington lifts the naval blockade, eases oil sanctions, and freezes new penalties; both sides enter a 60-day negotiation window. 

Iran, in return, commits not to build or acquire nuclear weapons—while keeping its current program intact.

A senior Iranian official summarized the substance to Reuters: the United States would release about $25 billion in frozen Iranian assets, including through direct cash transfers, regional mechanisms, and credit lines.

In exchange, Iran maintains what it calls the “status quo” on its nuclear program. No dismantlement. No rollback. Just time.

“Until there is a sincere commitment to restoring trust, Iran’s response will not change,” parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote earlier this week.

The structure resembles a financial bridge loan dressed as diplomacy. Immediate liquidity for Tehran, deferred obligations for everyone else.

For Israel, the concerns are less abstract. Reopening Hormuz restores hundreds of millions of dollars in daily revenue to Iran. The nuclear file remains unresolved, with enrichment capacity untouched. 

In Lebanon, Iranian officials are already calling for a comprehensive cease-fire, a move that could reframe any Israeli de-escalation as a strategic gain for Hezbollah.

And yet, even the existence of the deal is unstable.

Iran’s Fars News Agency reported that the decision is “still under legal, political and technical review.” 

The Foreign Ministry stated that “we will not sign today.” Analyst Mohammad Marandi wrote that “there will be no negotiations for now.” All on the same day the agreement was expected to materialize.

A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran. Iran’s foreign minister departed for Pakistan. According to Al Arabiya, the memorandum was to be signed digitally by Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf and U.S. Vice President Vance.

Israel has described the process as a “virtual agreement” with little practical substance, and a potential inflection point in U.S.–Israel relations.

The result is a deal that functions more as a signal than a settlement: money begins to move, pressure partially lifts, and the hardest questions are postponed.

Why Europe cannot replace what America is taking away 

What is unfolding across the Atlantic is being described in European defense circles as a "technical draining" of NATO's military foundation. The United States is preparing to significantly reduce its military footprint in Europe, withdrawing a substantial portion of the strategic assets that have long served as the backbone of the continent's defense. According to plans reportedly shared with NATO allies, Washington intends to cut nearly 30% of its deployed air power, including strategic bombers, fighter jets, aerial refueling tankers, maritime patrol aircraft, and a significant number of naval vessels and drones.

European officials have been informed that the US contribution could include a 30% reduction in strategic bombers, a 75% to 100% cut in certain reconnaissance and strike drones, and the withdrawal of approximately one-third of its fighter jets and half of its naval assets currently committed to European defense. This is not merely a reduction in troop numbers, but a targeted withdrawal of the high-end, game-changing capabilities that only the United States possesses.

For all the talk of European strategic autonomy, the continent cannot simply fill the void. European nations lack their own strategic bombers — a capability that has been a cornerstone of US escalation dominance for decades. They also do not produce fifth-generation fighter jets comparable to the F-35, nor do they have domestic alternatives for many of the specialized platforms being withdrawn, such as large transport aircraft and advanced aerial refueling tankers. Even where European systems exist, they often lack the range, payload, or integration capabilities of their American counterparts. 

What’s more, much of Europe's existing high-end military equipment, including the F-35 fighter jets flown by multiple nations, relies on US software, logistics, and even permission for re-export or deployment. Without US support, some of Europe's most advanced weapons could be rendered operationally useless. This means that even if Europe buys American to fill the gap, it remains dependent on Washington's political goodwill.

The coming months and years will likely see a two-speed Europe: an immediate, painful vulnerability as US assets depart, and a long-overdue, frantic effort to build a genuinely independent European defense industrial base. Whether that base can be built before the window of vulnerability closes is the central question facing the continent today.
